whyCorrect: The text sets up a contrast between two ages of fossil: hominins (found in Asia) and the much older early multicellular organisms of the Ediacaran period. The word "because" asks you to explain why scientists have to leave Asia and go to Mistaken Point to find those older specimens. The only reason that works is that the Mistaken Point formation is older than the hominin-bearing formation, so it is old enough to preserve Ediacaran life. Notice the passage already tells you Mistaken Point is an Ediacaran formation, so the blank has to state what that means: an earlier time period.

whyWrong.A: The text never says North America lacks early multicellular organisms; it says the opposite, that Mistaken Point has them. It also would not explain why scientists must go there.
whyWrong.B: How widely distributed each type of fossil is says nothing about age, and the sentence needs an age-based reason for looking at an older formation.
whyWrong.D: Mistaken Point is presented as an Ediacaran site, not a hominin site, and preservation quality of hominins is irrelevant to finding organisms that predate hominins.

commonMistakes: Treating "look elsewhere" as a question about geography when the logical gap is about time.
tips: When a blank follows "because," state the reason in the same terms the sentence itself introduced — here, age of the formation.

whyCorrect: Track exactly what the study measured: personality traits and music-preference factors, in participants from fifty-three countries on six continents. It found similar correlations between the two in all those places. The conclusion that follows is simply that the personality-to-preference link holds across cultures — people with the same personality profile like the same kinds of music no matter where they live. The blank should restate the finding's scope, not extend it to something untested.

whyWrong.A: The study assessed preferences for Western genres only, so it gives no basis for predicting preferences for non-Western styles whose characteristics differ.
whyWrong.B: This compares the finding to what "researchers had previously assumed," but the text reports no prior assumption about how much the relationship varies.
whyWrong.C: Familiarity with Western music was never measured; participants reported personality traits and preferences, not exposure.

commonMistakes: Picking the most impressive-sounding claim rather than the one the described data actually supports.

whyCorrect: "Lawyer and cycling advocate" has no article in front of it, which makes it a title-like description that attaches directly to the name, exactly like "biologist Jane Goodall." A restrictive appositive of that kind takes no punctuation at all, so the whole phrase reads as one subject: lawyer and cycling advocate Ernesto Hernandez-Lopez has identified. Any comma inside it would break the subject away from its verb.

whyWrong.A: A single comma after "advocate" opens a nonessential element that is never closed, and it splits the description from the name it belongs to.
whyWrong.B: Two commas would make the name nonessential information, which requires a determiner like "the" before the description; without one, the name is essential.
whyWrong.C: The comma after the name falls between the complete subject and the verb "has identified," which is never allowed.

tips: No "the" before a job title usually means no commas around the name that follows it.

whyCorrect: The blank sits inside a dash-enclosed aside that already has its own opening and closing dashes. Within that aside, "the languages Javanese and Bikol" is a single noun phrase: the names identify which languages, so nothing separates the noun from the names. No punctuation belongs in the blank.

whyWrong.B: A colon needs a complete sentence in front of it, and "The Austronesian language family comprises some 1,200 languages—including the languages" is not one.
whyWrong.C: A dash here would close the aside far too early, leaving the rest of the parenthetical and the second dash stranded.
whyWrong.D: A comma would mark "Javanese and Bikol" as nonessential, but those names are the essential identification of which languages are meant.

commonMistakes: Adding punctuation because the sentence looks crowded; the dashes are already doing that job.

whyCorrect: Look at what surrounds the blank: "efforts that, through community involvement and scientific ___ aim to bring." The comma right after "that" opens a modifying phrase, and every such phrase needs a closing comma before the sentence resumes with its verb, "aim." So the blank supplies that closing comma: efforts that, through community involvement and scientific study, aim to bring adjutants back.

whyWrong.A: With no comma, the opening comma after "that" is left unpaired and the modifier runs straight into the verb.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete sentence and introduce something; here it would cut the relative clause off from its own verb.
whyWrong.D: A hyphen joins parts of words; it cannot close an interrupting phrase.

tips: When you see a comma just before an interrupting phrase, check that a matching comma closes it.

whyCorrect: The main clause is already complete: "such de jure judicial independence became more prevalent." Everything after "as exemplified in Croatia's constitution" is description hanging off the noun "constitution," and that description starts with the participle "enacted." The word joined by "and" must be another participle, so the blank needs "containing" — a constitution enacted in 1991 and containing four of these features.

whyWrong.A: "Contained" as a past participle would have to be passive, but a constitution does not get "contained"; read as a finite verb it has no subject.
whyWrong.C: "Had contained" is a finite verb with no subject available, since "constitution" is already the object of the preposition "in."
whyWrong.D: "Contains" is likewise a finite verb with nothing to serve as its subject, so the sentence loses its structure.

commonMistakes: Assuming "constitution" can act as the subject of the verb in the blank; it is governed by the preposition "in."

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with "While," which makes everything up to the blank a subordinate clause that cannot stand alone. The rest — "more than 80 percent of this endangered stork species is found in Assam, India" — is the main clause. A subordinate clause that comes first is joined to the main clause with a comma.

whyWrong.A: No punctuation runs the subordinate clause straight into the main clause with nothing marking the break.
whyWrong.B: A period would leave "While the greater adjutant can be found...in Cambodia" standing alone as a fragment.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and "While..." is not independent.

tips: A leading "While," "Although," or "Because" clause takes a comma, never a semicolon or period.

whyCorrect: Split the sentence at the blank: "One might assume cases like this...to be rare" is a complete sentence, and "they are counted among a litany of examples of Stigler's law" is another. "On the contrary" is a transitional adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot fuse two sentences. You need a semicolon before it and a comma after it: rare; on the contrary, they are counted...

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation before "on the contrary," the two independent clauses run together.
whyWrong.B: This puts the comma and semicolon in the wrong order, splicing the first clause to the transition and then cutting the transition off from the clause it introduces.
whyWrong.C: Two commas around "on the contrary" leave the two independent clauses joined by nothing but a comma — a comma splice.

tips: Transitions like "however," "therefore," and "on the contrary" need a semicolon in front when they sit between two complete sentences.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states a general finding: negative adjectives get replaced faster than other words. The second sentence applies that finding to a specific pair — the negative adjective "illegal" versus the noun "crisis" — and predicts what should follow from it. That is a conclusion drawn from the rule, so the transition must signal result.

whyWrong.B: "Moreover" adds a second, separate piece of evidence, but the second sentence introduces no new finding; it derives a prediction from the first.
whyWrong.C: "Meanwhile" marks something happening alongside or in contrast, and there are no two simultaneous situations here.
whyWrong.D: "However" signals contrast, but the example agrees with the research finding rather than complicating it.

tips: If the second sentence could begin with "so," the transition is a result word.

whyCorrect: The two sentences describe different dates and different eclipse types: 1904 gave a total eclipse where the Moon blocks the Sun completely, and 1935 gave an annular eclipse where a ring of light remains. The relationship is a contrast between two kinds of event, so the transition has to set the second against the first.

whyWrong.A: "As a result" claims the 1935 eclipse was caused by the 1904 one, which the text never suggests.
whyWrong.C: "Simultaneously" would mean the two events happened at the same time, but they are thirty-one years apart.
whyWrong.D: "Indeed" reinforces or intensifies the previous statement, and an annular eclipse is a different phenomenon, not stronger evidence for a total one.

whyCorrect: The previous sentence has just told you where the sculpture is: on the wall of a university building. The sentence with the blank then describes how it looks and functions in that place. "There" points back to that location and lets the description continue in the same spot.

whyWrong.B: "Later" would signal a shift in time, but nothing in either sentence marks a sequence of events.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" would introduce a new example, yet this sentence is still discussing the same sculpture already named in the previous sentence.
whyWrong.D: "However" signals contrast, but the sentence confirms rather than complicates the point that Konrads's art blends into its surroundings.

whyCorrect: The stated goal is narrow: give the title of Hurston's first published short story. Only one choice actually pairs "first published short story" with the title "John Redding Goes to Sea." Everything the notes say about the year and the magazine is true but does not meet the goal, so a choice built out of those details fails no matter how accurate it is.

whyWrong.A: This gives the publication year and never states the title, which is the one thing the goal requires.
whyWrong.C: This supplies the year and the magazine but leaves the story unnamed.
whyWrong.D: This says the first work of fiction was a short story without naming it.

tips: Read the goal sentence first, then eliminate any choice that omits the specific item it names.

whyCorrect: The goal is to emphasize a difference between the two plants, so the sentence has to name both plants and state something true of one but not the other. Only one choice does that: it puts Pipturus albidus and Psidium cattleyanum side by side and separates them on native versus non-native status. The other options mention the plants without contrasting them, or discuss birds and seed dispersal instead.

whyWrong.A: This mentions only one of the two plants, so no comparison is made at all.
whyWrong.C: This describes the purpose of a study about birds and seed dispersal and never distinguishes the plants from each other.
whyWrong.D: This groups the two plants together as sharing the same trait, which is the opposite of emphasizing a difference.

commonMistakes: Choosing a sentence that mentions both plants without stating anything that separates them.

whyCorrect: The goal names one specific number to emphasize: Daniel Dias's gold medals. A sentence meets that goal only if it states the figure twenty-five and attaches it to Dias. One choice does exactly that, giving his total and then singling out the golds within it.

whyWrong.B: This gives debut years for both athletes and calls them multiple gold medalists without stating how many golds Dias won.
whyWrong.C: This is about Heinzmann and about what a gold medal signifies, not about Dias's count.
whyWrong.D: This gives Dias's thirty-eight total medals and his years of competition but never mentions gold.

tips: When the goal names a specific quantity, the correct sentence must contain that number.

whyCorrect: The sentence after the blank begins with "Instead" and says success usually comes through collaboration. That tells you the blank names the opposite of collaboration, matching the opening example of a prize going to a single person. "Solitary" means working alone, so recognition is not restricted to people who work by themselves.

whyWrong.B: "Coordinated" means working jointly, which is what "Instead" contrasts the blank with, so it reverses the logic.
whyWrong.C: "Considerate" describes being thoughtful toward others and has nothing to do with working alone or together.
whyWrong.D: "Coincidental" means happening by chance, which does not describe an individual scientist receiving a prize.

tips: Let "Instead" tell you the blank means the opposite of what follows.

whyCorrect: The narrator states the rule she was working under: she was supposed to memorize the whole piece. Right after "cheating" she explains what she did — looked up to see what notes followed instead of playing from memory. So "cheating" means she broke the requirement about how the piece was to be learned and performed, not that she wronged anyone.

whyWrong.B: No teacher appears in the passage and she is describing her private practicing, not an act aimed at fooling someone.
whyWrong.C: The contestants are never mentioned, and reading the music while practicing alone gains no advantage over anyone else.
whyWrong.D: She says she daydreamed and never listened, but nothing suggests she misjudged or misrepresented her own ability.

commonMistakes: Applying the everyday sense of "cheating" as deceiving a person, when the text defines it as skipping the memorization requirement.

whyCorrect: The colon after the blank means what follows defines it. What follows is "a diverse range of musical talents in different areas, from orchestral pieces and operas to popular film scores" — a list of unlike kinds of music. So the blank must mean covering many different types. "Varied" is that word.

whyWrong.A: "Outdated" would say the music is no longer current, and the sentence calls the body of work impressive, not obsolete.
whyWrong.B: "Lonely" describes a feeling a person has, not a property of a catalog of compositions.
whyWrong.C: "Forgotten" would mean nobody remembers the work, which contradicts the praise and has nothing to do with range.

tips: A colon promises a restatement — read past it before choosing.

whyCorrect: Two clues fix the blank. Forrest admired Faulkner and wrote the passage "in tribute" to him, and the part after the colon says anyone who knows Faulkner would see the resemblance. A passage that deliberately reproduces another writer's style is an imitation of it.

whyWrong.A: "Forgetting" is the opposite of a tribute that visibly resembles the original.
whyWrong.B: "Rejection" would mean Forrest turned away from Faulkner's style, but he admired it and reproduced it.
whyWrong.D: "Opinion" is a judgment about something, and an opinion of a style would not produce a visible resemblance in the prose.

whyCorrect: The shortcoming is the narrow focus on North America and Western Europe, and the sentence says it came partly from limited data. Then researchers gained access to records from India and Hungary — data from exactly the regions that were missing. Getting the missing data makes the problem smaller, so the blank means to reduce or relieve it.

whyWrong.A: "Presuppose" means to assume in advance, but the shortcoming already existed and was being corrected, not assumed.
whyWrong.B: "Categorize" means to sort into groups, which does nothing to address a gap in coverage.
whyWrong.C: "Validate" would mean confirming the narrow focus was justified, the opposite of what new data from Asia and Eastern Europe does.

commonMistakes: Reading the new data access as confirming the old research rather than fixing its gap.

whyCorrect: Map the text in two moves. First it introduces the survey and reports the gap in park use, 71.9% in Bogota against 35.7% in Fortaleza. Then the last sentence raises one candidate explanation — better access to nonpark amenities near parks — and rules it out, because Bogota respondents actually reported less such access. That is a proposal-then-rejection structure.

whyWrong.A: There is one study covering both cities, not two studies, and nothing in the second half corroborates the first.
whyWrong.C: The text never blames the survey method; it rejects an explanation about amenities, not about how data were collected.
whyWrong.D: No open question about park planning is posed, and the text ends by eliminating an explanation rather than answering anything.

tips: For structure questions, label what each sentence does before reading the choices.

whyCorrect: The text spends its first half on El Museo del Barrio — when it was founded, what it is dedicated to, how large its collection is — and its second half on the Emma S. Barrientos Mexican American Cultural Center and what that institution focuses on. Nothing is argued or compared; the passage simply describes each one and its subject area.

whyWrong.A: Funding and how artworks were purchased are never mentioned.
whyWrong.B: No historical development is traced; the passage gives founding facts, not a cause that produced these institutions.
whyWrong.D: Only El Museo del Barrio's collection size is given, so no contrast of sizes is possible.

commonMistakes: Choosing a choice with a strong verb like "trace" or "contrast" when the passage only reports.

whyCorrect: The passage tells you what is typical of Erdrich: everyday life in Ojibwe communities. Then "Yet" introduces the exceptions, and The Crown of Columbus is given as one — adventure fiction set largely on a Caribbean island. The stated difference is therefore the setting, outside an Ojibwe community.

whyWrong.A: No film adaptation is mentioned anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.C: The amount of dialogue is never discussed.
whyWrong.D: Having Ojibwe main characters would make the novel like her usual work, not different from it, and the text does not say who the characters are.

tips: "According to the text" means the answer must be stated, not merely plausible.

whyCorrect: Follow where the paragraph lands. It defines horizontal gene transfer, notes it is common among prokaryotes, then says it can increase antibiotic resistance and that knowing how to prevent it might help control dangerous pathogens. The final clause is the point: studying this process could produce a practical benefit.

whyWrong.A: No common perception is described, so nothing is being corrected.
whyWrong.B: The text says the process is common but never compares that to what anyone initially thought.
whyWrong.C: There is no new research and no earlier findings being challenged.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice that sounds like a research summary when the passage never mentions a study or a prior belief.

whyCorrect: The hypothesis is specific: the PCFG whales' smaller maximum size is an adaptation to the resource opportunities in their particular foraging range. To support it, a finding must tie being smaller to getting food in that range. A finding that PCFG whales feed in shallow rocky kelp beds that larger ENP whales physically cannot reach does exactly that — small size is what makes those resources usable.

whyWrong.A: Proximity to ports and cities is about human activity, not about food resources or body size.
whyWrong.C: Different prey species show the ranges differ, but nothing connects that difference to why a smaller maximum size would be advantageous.
whyWrong.D: Trends in average size over recent decades describe change over time, not an adaptation to the foraging environment.

tips: A support question needs the choice that links the two specific things the hypothesis links — here, small size and access to food.

whyCorrect: The student's word is "must account for" — that is a claim that IGF-1 variation is the explanation for size differences among breeds. To undermine it you do not need to show IGF-1 is irrelevant; you only need to show it is not the whole story. Stating that IGF-1's gene is one of several genes known to affect dog size does that directly, because then size variance cannot be attributed to IGF-1 variation alone.

whyWrong.A: That most breeds do not share one variant just confirms the gene varies widely, which fits the student's conclusion rather than weakening it.
whyWrong.B: This limits how far the findings generalize to other species, but the student's claim is only about dogs.
whyWrong.C: This says the variations do produce substantial size variance, which supports the student instead of undermining them.

tips: Undermining an "X explains Y" claim usually means showing something else also explains Y.

whyCorrect: The claim is narrow: Vanya feels the professor does not appreciate him. Look for a quotation where Vanya says he worked for the professor and got no recognition for it. The line about managing the estate for twenty-five years, sending the returns "like the most honest of servants," and never receiving "one single word of thanks" states both halves of that claim.

whyWrong.B: This is Serebrakoff speaking about his own life and mortality; it says nothing about how he treats Vanya's work.
whyWrong.C: Vanya attacks the professor's scholarship as worthless, which shows contempt for the professor's achievements, not a sense that his own labor went unthanked.
whyWrong.D: This shows Vanya's disillusionment with the professor's career amounting to "a blank," again a judgment of the professor rather than a complaint about being unappreciated.

commonMistakes: Choosing any quotation where Vanya criticizes the professor, when the claim is specifically about Vanya's own work going unrecognized.

whyCorrect: The researchers' point is that climate change moves species into new ranges and makes previously unlivable areas habitable. If where a species belongs keeps shifting, then labeling one species native and another invasive rests on a fixed picture that no longer holds. The blank should state that general consequence: these classifications may not match the changing conditions.

whyWrong.A: International coordination is a policy recommendation the text never raises; the passage is about whether the categories still work.
whyWrong.B: Nothing singles out the Gaboon viper as the one case where the distinction fails; the concern applies to such classifications generally.
whyWrong.D: The text says the viper could outcompete native species in South Africa, not that vipers once lived there and were driven out.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states the purpose of the experiments: to better understand people living with PTSD. The findings are about why distressing memories persist for years. The contribution these results are expected to make therefore has to be to humans with PTSD, and the concrete form that takes is better treatment for them.

whyWrong.B: The mice were a model for studying human PTSD; understanding PTSD in the mice themselves is not the stated aim.
whyWrong.C: The connection between memory neurons in the prefrontal cortex is presented as already known and used to explain the result, so it cannot be the contribution the result makes.
whyWrong.D: More animal studies would be a next step in method, not the contribution the passage sets up with its opening purpose.

tips: When a text opens by naming its purpose, the conclusion usually returns to that purpose.

whyCorrect: "British artist" carries no article, so it works as a title attached directly to the name, like "British artist Chris Killip." That kind of description and name form one unit and take no punctuation between them.

whyWrong.A: A colon has to follow a complete sentence, and "A pet rabbit is held...by British artist" is not one at that point.
whyWrong.B: A dash marks a break or an aside, but the name is the necessary completion of "by British artist," not an interruption.
whyWrong.D: A comma would make the name nonessential, which requires a determiner such as "the" before the description.

tips: Description with no "the" plus a name equals no punctuation.

whyCorrect: Read both halves. "Some of these appear as lists" is a complete sentence, and "in 'Things That Arouse a Fond Memory of the Past,' Shonagon catalogs her appreciation for pressed silk, a moonlit night, and dried hollyhock" is another complete sentence that gives an example of those lists. A colon after a complete sentence is the right way to introduce that example.

whyWrong.B: With no punctuation, the second complete clause runs straight into the first with nothing separating them.
whyWrong.C: The colon lands after "in," cutting a preposition off from the title it governs.
whyWrong.D: A comma joining two complete sentences is a comma splice.

commonMistakes: Assuming a colon must be followed by a list; it can introduce an explanation or example just as well.

whyCorrect: Everything up to "respectively" is one complete sentence about when the two paintings were finished, and "such allegorical artwork was particularly popular from the 15th through the late 18th centuries" is a second complete sentence. Two independent clauses with no conjunction between them need a semicolon, and "respectively" belongs with the dates it refers to, set off by a comma.

whyWrong.B: This ends the first clause with a comma and splices the two sentences together.
whyWrong.C: It drops the comma before "respectively" and still joins the two independent clauses with only a comma.
whyWrong.D: Putting the semicolon before "respectively" strands that word at the head of the second clause, where it has no pair of items to refer to.

whyCorrect: The sentence is building a three-item list of temperature readings, and the third item is already printed after the blank as the 8:30 p.m. reading joined by "and." So the blank has to supply the first two items with commas after each: the 3:00 p.m. reading, then the 5:00 p.m. reading, then a comma leading into "and." No comma belongs between a temperature and the time it was taken, because the time is not a separate list item.

whyWrong.A: Commas inside each item split the reading from its time, and periods would break the list into fragments.
whyWrong.C: Without a comma at the end, the second item runs into "and 16.2" as if two readings were one item.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon separates list items only when the items themselves contain commas, which these do not, and it cannot sit in front of "and" here.

tips: Punctuate each reading-plus-time as one unbroken item, then separate the items.

whyCorrect: Strip out the interrupting clause between the commas and the sentence reads "The chapter ___ known as Doo Alk'ai." The subject is "chapter," singular, and the surrounding sentences describe a present, ongoing fact, so the verb is "is." The plural noun "acres" sitting right before the blank belongs to the modifier, not to the subject.

whyWrong.A: "Are" is plural and agrees with nothing in the sentence; the subject is the singular "chapter."
whyWrong.B: "Have been" is plural as well, and the present perfect wrongly suggests a period of time rather than a current fact.
whyWrong.C: "Were" is both plural and past, and the chapter is still known by that name.

tips: Cross out anything between commas before checking subject-verb agreement.

whyCorrect: The blank starts a "from...to..." range: from one reading at 11:00 a.m. to another at 7:00 p.m. Nothing in that construction gets punctuation — "from" attaches straight to its object, and the object attaches straight to the time it was taken. So the blank takes "from" plus the temperature plus "at" with no commas at all.

whyWrong.A: The comma after "from" separates the preposition from its object.
whyWrong.B: It adds that same wrong comma and a second one that cuts "at" off from the time it introduces.
whyWrong.D: A colon cannot follow a preposition, and the trailing comma again splits "at" from its time.

commonMistakes: Adding a comma because the sentence is long; a preposition never takes one before its object.

whyCorrect: The previous sentence reports a success: NASA moved a moonlet's orbit. The sentence with the blank reports a limit on that success — nobody has shown the same works on a primary object like 2004 DC. That is a reversal of expectation, so the transition has to be concessive.

whyWrong.B: "For example" would make the second sentence an instance of the first, but a gap in the evidence is not an example of a successful test.
whyWrong.C: "Likewise" claims the two statements match, when one is a success and the other is an unproven case.
whyWrong.D: "Moreover" adds a further supporting point, and this sentence qualifies rather than reinforces.

tips: A sentence built on "have yet to" almost always needs a contrast word.

whyCorrect: The second sentence uses the past perfect, "had served," which places that presidency before the 1990 appointment just described. The transition needs to mark that step backward in time.

whyWrong.A: "In conclusion" signals the end of an argument, but this sentence adds an earlier fact rather than summing anything up.
whyWrong.C: "Thus" claims the NSBP presidency resulted from the National Science Foundation appointment, which reverses the order the verb tense establishes.
whyWrong.D: "For example" would make the presidency an instance of the 1990 directorship, but they are two separate posts.

tips: "Had" plus a past participle is a signal that the sentence is reaching further back in time.

whyCorrect: The paragraph makes a claim, admits something against it, then reasserts the claim. The blank sits at the admission: archways and mosaics obviously cannot grow in a forest. The next sentence opens with "Still," which is the signal that a concession has just been made, so the blank must be the word that grants that point.

whyWrong.B: "Thus" would present the sentence as a consequence of the architects championing nature, but it undercuts that claim instead.
whyWrong.C: "Furthermore" adds support, and this sentence raises a complication.
whyWrong.D: "Similarly" claims a parallel between the two sentences, when the second pushes back against the first.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the "Still," in the following sentence, which is the clearest clue that the blank concedes a point.

whyCorrect: The goal names one thing to include: when the theory was published. Only one choice states the date, 1037 CE, and attaches it to the publication of the landmass theory. The other options are all accurate but leave out the one detail the goal demands.

whyWrong.B: This mentions the theory but gives no publication date.
whyWrong.C: This only identifies who al-Biruni was and never mentions the theory or its date.
whyWrong.D: This describes the theory and the scholar but says nothing about when it was published.

tips: If the goal asks "when," scan the choices for a date and eliminate every choice without one.

whyCorrect: To emphasize size, the sentence must state a measurement. Only one choice gives Tlaxcoapan's area, roughly 42 square kilometers, and identifies which place that area belongs to. Every other choice is about what a municipality does or where Tlaxcoapan sits administratively.

whyWrong.A: This is about street lighting as a public service and never mentions Tlaxcoapan or any measurement.
whyWrong.C: This places Tlaxcoapan among Hidalgo's municipalities, which is a count of regions, not a statement of Tlaxcoapan's size.
whyWrong.D: This describes the services Tlaxcoapan provides and omits its area entirely.

tips: "Emphasize the size" means the sentence has to carry the number.

whyCorrect: The goal is to indicate the title of the award-winning novel, so the sentence has to contain both the title and the award. Only one choice names Babel-17 and states that it won a Nebula Award. The others refer to a novel without naming it.

whyWrong.A: This calls a novel one of the best works of science fiction but never gives its title.
whyWrong.B: This describes Delaney as award-winning and names no novel at all.
whyWrong.D: This gives the publication year of an unnamed novel and never mentions the award.

whyCorrect: The sentence defines its own term: boredom "creates an anxious tension" when there is nowhere to fix your attention. The phrase "not somnolence but ___" then asks for the opposite of sleepiness, and the word has to name that anxious tension. "Perturbation" means agitation or unease, which is exactly what was just described.

whyWrong.A: "Fortitude" is courage under hardship, which has nothing to do with restless attention.
whyWrong.C: "Nonchalance" is unbothered calm, the opposite of the anxious tension the sentence describes.
whyWrong.D: "Indolence" is laziness, which sits on the same side as somnolence and so cannot be what the sentence contrasts with it.

tips: In a "not X but Y" frame, Y must oppose X — eliminate any word that is a near synonym of X.

whyCorrect: The adverb "eagerly" tells you the word describes a feeling, and the object is "the moment when he would be at home again" — something still in the future. Wanting a future moment to arrive is looking forward to it.

whyWrong.A: "Describing" would make the Mole narrate the moment, but he is hurrying toward it, not talking about it.
whyWrong.B: "Getting ahead of" is another real sense of "anticipate," but you cannot get ahead of a moment you are hurrying to reach, and it would not pair with "eagerly."
whyWrong.D: "Instructing" makes no sense with a moment as its object.

commonMistakes: Choosing a dictionary meaning of the word that the sentence's own context does not support.

whyCorrect: The paragraph is about where features of Puerto Rican Spanish came from — words from Taino, contributions from African languages. The example then links certain vowel pronunciations back to Yoruba. The blank names that act of following a feature back to its source, so "traced to" is the fit.

whyWrong.B: "Announced" describes making something public and cannot take "to how they are pronounced" as its object.
whyWrong.C: "Offered to" would mean presenting the pronunciation as a gift, which is nonsense here.
whyWrong.D: "Surrendered to" means yielding, not deriving from a source.

whyCorrect: The shortcoming is the narrow focus on a few North American and Western European countries, caused partly by missing data. The second sentence then says researchers gained access to records from Brazil and Russia — data from exactly the regions that had been left out. Getting that data reduces the problem, so the blank must mean to lessen it.

whyWrong.A: "Validate" would mean confirming the narrow focus was sound, the opposite of correcting it.
whyWrong.B: "Presuppose" means to assume beforehand, but the shortcoming was an existing flaw being addressed.
whyWrong.C: "Categorize" means to sort into groups, which would not reduce a gap in coverage.

whyCorrect: The flaw described is a focus limited to a few North American and Western European countries, driven by scarce data. New administrative records from Ivory Coast and Poland supply exactly what was missing, so the researchers' action makes the flaw less severe. "Ameliorate" means to make a bad situation better.

whyWrong.A: "Postulate" means to propose as a starting assumption, but the shortcoming is an established problem, not a proposal.
whyWrong.C: "Sanction" means to approve or authorize, which would endorse the flaw rather than reduce it.
whyWrong.D: "Rationalize" means to invent a justification for something, and gaining new data corrects the gap instead of excusing it.

commonMistakes: Reading the sentence as researchers defending the old research rather than fixing it.

whyCorrect: Follow the timeline the passage builds: bottles buried in 1879, bottles retrieved in periodic checks, results after 60 years, and another bottle dug up in 2021. The present tense in "researchers are conducting" and the 2021 retrieval both signal the experiment has not ended. The text's job is to lay out that long-running study.

whyWrong.B: Nothing here is about eliminating plants; the experiment tests how long buried seeds stay able to germinate.
whyWrong.C: Only one experiment appears, Beal's, so there is nothing to compare it with.
whyWrong.D: The passage reports results about seed viability but never discusses difficulties in preserving seeds.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences set up an apparent split: privately owned libraries with restricted access, then the first public libraries. The word "however" and Fernandes's point reverse that split — both kinds of owner treated their libraries as extensions of personal patronage. The passage exists to land that claim of underlying similarity, with the scale being the only real difference.

whyWrong.A: The text never claims private libraries disappeared, so it is not correcting that idea.
whyWrong.B: No judgment is made about emperors having too much influence; the point is about how both groups viewed their libraries.
whyWrong.C: Public access during the republican period is the setup, not the purpose, and the passage moves past it to Fernandes's argument.

tips: The sentence after "however" usually carries the main purpose.

whyCorrect: "Reductive" means a model boils something complicated down to too little. The energy ladder makes fuel choice depend mainly on one thing, household income. Heltberg's Guatemala study found use that was heterogeneous and flexible and shaped by several factors, including local prices. So the criticism is one cause versus many.

whyWrong.A: This says households ignore income entirely, but Heltberg's finding was that income is one factor among several, not that it drops out.
whyWrong.B: The displacement of one fuel by another is a detail of the model, and the text never claims fuel types are used in equal proportion.
whyWrong.C: The study is presented as showing fuel choice is complex generally, not as contrasting Guatemala's factors with Costa Rica's.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice that overstates the study's result into a flat denial of income's role.

whyCorrect: The turning point is the viaduct at Point du Jour, which the narrator says "blocked the river" and marks "the end of Paris, the beginning of the country." Past it, the Seine spreads out "as though it had regained space and liberty" and becomes "the peaceful river." Saying the river regained space and peace only makes sense if it lacked both while it ran through the city, so the passage contrasts a constrained, unquiet urban river with an open, calm rural one.

whyWrong.A: This reverses the passage: the calm stretch begins after the arches, and the text never describes a heavy current at them.
whyWrong.B: The passage draws a contrast between the city stretch and the country stretch rather than likening the river to Paris, and it says nothing about beauty or slow change.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text concerns how clear or murky the water is; the change described is in width and calm.

commonMistakes: Reading "blocked the river" as a description of turbulence rather than as the boundary between city and country.

whyCorrect: The text names a specific benefit of historical DNA: access to genomic data from extirpated populations — groups that no longer exist in a place. Data from a population that is gone cannot come from sampling living organisms, so hDNA opens a door other genomic sources cannot. The rest of the passage explains why it is still underused, which does not change that benefit.

whyWrong.B: The bat pathogen work is one example of its use, not evidence about which researchers have gained most from hDNA overall.
whyWrong.C: The stated reason for underuse is degradation and the limits of current extraction methods, not any controversy.
whyWrong.D: The text says hDNA is often degraded but never compares its degradation to that of other DNA of similar age.

tips: "Unique benefits, such as..." is the sentence doing the work — the answer should restate what follows it.

whyCorrect: The claim has two parts: the house is remote and it stands alone. You need a quotation that shows nothing else nearby. The description of seeing "nothing but the great gray prairie on every side" with "not a tree nor a house" in view gives both emptiness and isolation directly.

whyWrong.A: This describes a forest and a rocky hill in Oz, not the Kansas house.
whyWrong.B: This is a dream about Aunt Em welcoming Dorothy home and says nothing about the house's surroundings.
whyWrong.C: This names who lives there and what Uncle Henry does; "the midst of the great Kansas prairies" hints at open country but describes no isolation of the house itself.

commonMistakes: Settling for a quotation that mentions Kansas rather than one that shows the house standing alone.

whyCorrect: The last sentence tells you what the vocal manipulation does: it invites listeners to reflect on how far digital technology shapes human experience today. Prompting reflection about the present-day role of technology in people's lives is a remark about the conditions people live under now, which is what "commentary on contemporary social conditions" means.

whyWrong.A: The text says the practice prompts reflection on technology's reach; it never judges that reach as harmful.
whyWrong.B: The passage stresses what is distinctive about experience today, not what has stayed the same across history.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the text is about music changing how listeners see themselves; the reflection is about technology's role in experience generally.

commonMistakes: Reading "invites reflection" as implying criticism, and choosing the negative option.

whyCorrect: Walsh's finding has two links in it: users become aware that others may see their listening, and that awareness changes what they actually do. The quotation you want has to show both. Choosing songs based on what followers might want to see rather than what you feel like hearing is exactly awareness of being observed changing behavior.

whyWrong.A: This is about the recommendation algorithm repeating itself, which involves no audience and no change in behavior.
whyWrong.B: This compares streaming to buying records and describes passivity, not self-consciousness about being watched.
whyWrong.C: This describes enjoying a shared experience with friends but does not show the user altering what they listen to because of how it might be perceived.

tips: When a finding has two parts, the illustrating quotation must contain both.

whyCorrect: Three facts are stacked: Scottish dialects emphasize "r" in certain positions, Upland South dialects emphasize it in the same positions, and the Upland South was settled largely by people of Scottish descent. The settlement fact supplies the direction of influence — the feature travelled with the settlers, so the Upland South dialects got it from Scotland.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text concerns future spread of the feature to other regions.
whyWrong.C: This reverses the direction; the migration ran from Scotland to the Upland South, not the other way.
whyWrong.D: The whole point is that the emphasis on "r" is present in the Upland South, so it was not abandoned.

tips: When a passage gives a migration fact, it is usually there to fix which way the influence ran.

whyCorrect: Apply the stated rule: sounds a listener finds meaningful are perceived as quieter than sounds of equal volume the listener treats as noise. The researchers suspect participants treated the nature sounds as noise, while the music is the meaningful sound. At the same 61.5 decibels, then, the nature sounds would seem louder than the song even though the two are physically equal.

whyWrong.A: If the nature sounds already seemed louder, a participant would turn them down, not up.
whyWrong.B: The rule concerns which sound seems louder, not whether listeners can judge an absolute decibel figure.
whyWrong.D: The setup depends on the nature sounds being treated as meaningless; calling both comparably meaningful contradicts the premise the inference rests on.

commonMistakes: Losing track of which sound counts as "noise" — here it is the nature recordings, not the music.

whyCorrect: Look at what opens the interrupting phrase: an em dash right after "efforts that." A dash used to set off an aside has to be matched by a second dash when the sentence resumes with its verb, "aim." So the blank closes the pair with another dash.

whyWrong.A: A comma cannot close a phrase that a dash opened; the two marks must match.
whyWrong.C: A colon does not close an interruption, and it would cut the relative clause off from its verb.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation at all, the opening dash is never closed and the modifier runs into "aim."

tips: Whatever mark opens an interrupting phrase must be the mark that closes it.

whyCorrect: Find where one complete sentence ends and the next begins. "Brothers Andre and Edoward Michelin sought to increase profits...visiting the guide's recommended hotels and restaurants" is complete on its own, and "as it grew in scope and influence, the guide had its modest French eateries replaced..." is a second complete sentence with its own subject and verb. Two independent clauses with no coordinating conjunction between them require a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: With nothing in the blank the two complete sentences run together.
whyWrong.C: "And" with no comma before it fuses the two independent clauses; a coordinating conjunction joining full clauses needs a comma in front of it.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

tips: Test each side of the blank for a subject and a verb before choosing a mark.

whyCorrect: Remove the clause between the commas and the sentence is "Alicia Perez-Porro ___ as a biologist at the Smithsonian Institution." That subject is one person, so the verb takes the singular present form, "works." The plural "sea sponges" just before the blank belongs to the modifier and has no effect on the verb.

whyWrong.A: "Work" is the plural present form and does not agree with a single person.
whyWrong.C: "Are working" is plural, and the progressive is unnecessary for a standing job description.
whyWrong.D: "Have worked" is plural as well; the singular would be "has worked."

commonMistakes: Letting the plural noun nearest the blank decide the verb form.

whyCorrect: The part before the comma is already a complete sentence: the impact of PNPs belies their minuscule size. What follows can only be a modifier attached to it, not a second sentence, because there is no conjunction or semicolon. "Ranging" makes that stretch a participial phrase describing the nanoparticles.

whyWrong.A: "Range" gives the second half its own subject and verb, splicing two sentences with a comma.
whyWrong.B: "Can range" is likewise a finite verb and produces the same comma splice.
whyWrong.D: "Will range" is finite too, and the future tense also clashes with a fact that is true now.

tips: After a complete sentence and a comma, an -ing form is usually what a modifier needs.

whyCorrect: Two items follow the blank — median salary and work-life balance — so the noun before them must be plural, "metrics." And the salary and balance belong to the one profession under discussion, so the possessive is the singular "profession's."

whyWrong.B: "Metric" is singular but two metrics are named.
whyWrong.C: "Professions'" is a plural possessive, yet only one profession is being ranked.
whyWrong.D: This is singular where a plural is needed and drops the possessive entirely, leaving "the professions median salary."

commonMistakes: Choosing the possessive form by sound; count the things being possessed and the owners separately.

whyCorrect: The blank is the verb of the clause after "yet," whose subject is "the building itself." That clause needs a finite verb in the same past tense as "We came" in the first half. "Impressed" is singular past and completes the sentence.

whyWrong.A: "To impress" is an infinitive and leaves the clause after "yet" without a verb.
whyWrong.B: "Have impressed" is plural and does not agree with the singular "building."
whyWrong.D: "Impressing" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the clause never gets a predicate.

whyCorrect: The first sentence claims Chaucer pioneered literary use of Middle English. The second backs that claim with hard evidence — over 2,000 first documented uses, and a contemporary calling him "the first finder of our fair language." The transition should signal that the second sentence confirms and strengthens the first.

whyWrong.A: "However" signals contrast, but the evidence agrees with the claim.
whyWrong.B: "That being said" introduces a qualification, and nothing here qualifies the previous point.
whyWrong.C: "Besides" adds a separate consideration alongside the first; this sentence supplies proof of the very claim just made.

whyCorrect: Both halves of the sentence do the same job: each names a poem that meditates on a specific painting, first Alexander on Alston's Walking, then Eady on Lawrence's Summer Street Scene. The second example matches the first, so the transition marks similarity.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" would mark the second poem as an exception, but it fits the pattern exactly.
whyWrong.B: "Conversely" sets up an opposite case, and there is no opposition between two ekphrastic poems.
whyWrong.D: "Hence" claims the second poem follows as a consequence of the first, which the text does not suggest.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states a need: with demand for region-specific artisanal cheeses came the need to guarantee those claims to consumers. The second sentence reports the EU creating DOP status, a label that certifies exactly those claims. The action answers the need, so the transition must show result.

whyWrong.A: "Conversely" introduces an opposite, but the DOP label satisfies the need rather than opposing it.
whyWrong.B: "Likewise" would mean the second sentence parallels the first, when it is the response to it.
whyWrong.C: "Regardless" would mean the EU acted despite the need described, which reverses the relationship.

tips: A stated problem followed by an action taken almost always calls for a result transition.

whyCorrect: To emphasize location, the sentence has to make the place the point, not a passing detail. The choice that says visitors will have to travel to Deer Isle, Maine, builds the whole sentence around where the complex is. Other choices may contain the place name, but they put it in a modifier while the main statement is about the architect or the design.

whyWrong.B: This is about architectural style and the cedar-shingled buildings, with no location at all.
whyWrong.C: Deer Isle appears only as part of a phrase identifying the building; the sentence is about who designed it.
whyWrong.D: This names the architect and describes the buildings and never says where they are.

tips: "Emphasize X" means X should be what the main clause is about, not a detail tucked inside it.

whyCorrect: The notes give one thing the two birds share — both are found on the Galapagos Island of Floreana — and one thing that separates them sharply, their weights. To emphasize a similarity you need the shared fact stated about both birds in the same sentence, which only the choice naming both species on Floreana does.

whyWrong.A: This puts 2.5 kilograms against 9 grams, which emphasizes a difference, not a similarity.
whyWrong.B: This describes only the finch, so no similarity is asserted.
whyWrong.D: This mentions the penguin alone and leaves the finch out, so the two birds are never linked.

commonMistakes: Choosing the sentence that mentions both birds' weights; sharing a location is the similarity, and the weights are the contrast.

whyCorrect: The goal asks for a cause, so the sentence needs the toxicity and the reason for it joined together. The notes supply that reason: the water is three to eight times saltier than the surrounding ocean, and that extreme saltiness is what makes it toxic. Only one choice states both halves and links them with "because."

whyWrong.A: This reports that the pools are toxic and when they were discovered, never saying why.
whyWrong.C: This is about the discovery and claims the pools host diverse marine life, which contradicts the note that they are toxic to most sea life.
whyWrong.D: This defines a brine pool without mentioning toxicity or its cause.

tips: When the goal starts with "explain why," the answer nearly always contains a causal word.

whyCorrect: The colon introduces the numbers that define the blank: nine consonants in Sikaiana, eight in Hawaiian, against a global median above twenty-two. Those counts are far below typical, so the blank means unusually small. "Minimal" fits the comparison the sentence sets up.

whyWrong.B: "Static" means unchanging over time, but the sentence compares sizes of inventories, not their stability.
whyWrong.C: "Replicable" means able to be reproduced, which says nothing about how many consonants a language has.
whyWrong.D: "Melodic" describes how a language sounds, and the evidence given is a count, not a quality of sound.

tips: When numbers follow a colon, ask what they measure — that is what the blank must describe.

whyCorrect: The colon spells out the meaning: a "constantly evolving network" whose channels and land "change in size and shape" as sediment is deposited. The blank must name that ongoing change, and "dynamic" is the word for something continually in motion.

whyWrong.A: "Immutable" means incapable of change, which directly contradicts the description after the colon.
whyWrong.B: "Unrivaled" would claim the delta is better than all others, but the sentence opens with "As with other river deltas," grouping it with them.
whyWrong.C: "Sustainable" concerns whether something can be maintained over time and does not describe constant physical change.

whyCorrect: The previous sentence stretches from monumental sculpture in a park to street murals, and ends with "everything from...to...." That range is why the city "can thus satisfy any art lover." The blank has to name the wide variety, so "breadth of" is what the argument needs.

whyWrong.A: "Controversy over" introduces disagreement, which is never mentioned and would not explain satisfying every art lover.
whyWrong.C: "Apathy toward" means indifference, the opposite of an outstanding collection people come to see.
whyWrong.D: "Confusion about" adds a problem where the sentence is drawing a positive conclusion.

tips: "Thus" means the blank must be the reason for the claim that follows it.

whyCorrect: The clause after "since" gives the reason: weeks or months of hard, physically tiring work to clear dirt and rock off the specimen. That describes effort and hardship, so the blank must mean demanding. "Difficult" is the word supported by the evidence given.

whyWrong.A: "Cheap" concerns cost, and nothing in the sentence mentions money.
whyWrong.B: "Rapid" contradicts a process that takes weeks or months.
whyWrong.C: "Common" describes how often something happens, not how hard it is, and frequency is never discussed.

whyCorrect: The colon gives the evidence: knowledge spillovers drive clustering in one case, while tube manufacturers collocate "for different reasons." So the mix of causes is not the same from one industry to the next. "Heterogeneous" means varied or made of unlike parts, which is exactly that finding.

whyWrong.A: "Credible" judges whether a claim is believable, not whether causes differ between industries.
whyWrong.C: "Imperative" means necessary or urgent, which does not describe a mix of factors.
whyWrong.D: "Decisive" would say the factors settle the matter, but the point is that they vary from industry to industry.

commonMistakes: Skipping the clause after the colon, which is the only place the sentence says what the blank means.

whyCorrect: Read the line the phrase sits in: the friend's soul is calm "by the lack of anvil and strife." The anvil is the hammering of labor and "strife" is conflict, and both are named only as things that are absent. They function as the noisy, punishing world set against the quiet the friend is enjoying now, which the kestrel muting its note then reinforces.

whyWrong.A: The phrase names what the friend is free of, and his calm comes from that freedom, so it cannot show him valuing work and conflict.
whyWrong.B: The unspoken closeness is established by the earlier lines about deeper content never being spoken, not by this image.
whyWrong.C: Nature is on the same side as the friends here, providing the sweet silence they share; the poem sets no opposition between them.

tips: Watch for a word like "lack" — it turns an image into a description of what is missing.

whyCorrect: The passage moves from what Joplin is known for to a complaint that listeners "will miss the full range of Joplin's creativity" by ignoring his other works, then gives two examples and closes by saying they "deserve as much fame as Joplin's biggest hits." That final sentence is a recommendation, which makes the text an argument for attending to the lesser-known pieces.

whyWrong.B: Ragtime and classical are mentioned only as elements Joplin blended; no comparison of ragtime and opera is developed.
whyWrong.C: How Joplin learned to compose or perform is never discussed.
whyWrong.D: The text is about one composer's overlooked catalog, not about broadening listening across composers.

tips: A closing sentence containing "should" or "deserve" usually marks an argument, not a description.

whyCorrect: The text assigns each research team one result. Brown's team found lunar intensity negatively associated with foraging in Arizona pocket mice; Curtis's team found it positively associated with foraging in mongoose lemurs. A positive association means the two rise together, so more moonlight goes with more foraging by the lemurs.

whyWrong.A: This is the explanation the passage offers afterward using optimal foraging theory, not the finding Curtis's team made.
whyWrong.C: The lemurs' greater reliance on vision is given as a standing trait used to explain the result, not something measured as changing with moonlight.
whyWrong.D: That is Brown's finding about the mice, not Curtis's.

commonMistakes: Attributing the passage's interpretation of a result to the researchers who produced the result.

whyCorrect: Follow the chain the text builds: Pimentel's study used a mean sample of only 12 fish, Clark's review warns that such small samples increase the potential for biased analysis, and biased analysis can produce reports of exaggerated effects. The suggestion is therefore that Pimentel's strong effect may be overstated. None of the three substantive choices says that, so none of them is supported.

whyWrong.A: The text never compares Pimentel's sample size with the sample sizes of earlier studies; it only calls 12 relatively small.
whyWrong.B: Nothing extends the conclusion to other fish species, and the passage casts doubt on the conclusion rather than widening it.
whyWrong.D: Clark's review raises a methodological caution about sample size; it does not report results from similar studies that overturned Pimentel's finding.

commonMistakes: Reading a warning about method as evidence that other studies contradicted the result.

whyCorrect: The researcher's claim is about time: a ten-year-old survey may no longer describe how far today's residents would walk. The passage already tells you that willingness to walk depends on things like paved sidewalks and crosswalks. So evidence that those features changed substantially in the neighborhood over the same ten years gives a concrete reason the old answers no longer apply.

whyWrong.B: Weather affecting transit use says nothing about whether the neighborhood has changed since the survey was taken.
whyWrong.C: More cyclists on the roads is a change, but the passage never lists cycling among the factors that affect willingness to walk to transit.
whyWrong.D: Satisfaction of current riders with existing stops is unrelated to the accuracy of a survey about walking distance in this neighborhood.

tips: To attack a dated survey, look for a choice showing that something the survey depended on has since changed.

whyCorrect: The claim has two parts: Winnemucca speaks straight to the reader, and she does it to assert her authority. The line beginning "My dear reader" does both — it addresses the reader directly and then asserts that her decades of experience mean "I know what I am talking about."

whyWrong.B: This admits uncertainty about her own birth year, which works against a claim of authority rather than for it, and it addresses no reader.
whyWrong.C: This addresses readers but reports where the soldiers went; it makes no claim about her knowledge or reliability.
whyWrong.D: This addresses readers while confessing she cannot describe the scene, which asks for their imagination instead of asserting her credibility.

commonMistakes: Picking any quotation containing "dear readers"; the address alone does not establish authority.

whyCorrect: The load-bearing detail is the clause in the dash: the temperature difference between fruiting and nonfruiting sites of the mycelium "persisted even after fruited bodies were detached." If the difference survives removal of the fruited bodies, then whatever produces it is not the fruited bodies themselves. That is exactly what it means for the variation to occur independent of their presence.

whyWrong.B: It reverses the finding — fruiting sites were colder, not warmer, so no correlation between higher temperature and productivity is reported.
whyWrong.C: Depth and spread of the mycelium in soil are never mentioned as a cause; the text offers no explanation for the difference.
whyWrong.D: The text says both fruited bodies and mycelium stay below ambient temperature but never compares the two with each other.

tips: A detail set off by dashes is usually the one the question turns on.

whyCorrect: The study found one clear split: glossy ibises prefer deeper breeding-season water, and small dark herons do not share that preference. A management strategy that deepens the water therefore matches what one species wants and not the other, so it should draw ibises more than herons.

whyWrong.B: Birds that do not live in wetlands were never studied, and deepening wetland water gives no reason to expect them.
whyWrong.C: Lifespan was not measured; the research was about how birds choose where to live.
whyWrong.D: Deeper water is stated as a preference of glossy ibises, so it cannot reduce the area's appeal to them.

commonMistakes: Treating "not true for small dark herons" as meaning herons avoid deep water, when it only means they show no such preference.

whyCorrect: Line the three studies up. Undisturbed waters show the carbon-mercury association; wastewater-affected waters do not, which prompted the guess that the association only holds where humans have not interfered; then urban-disturbed waters show the association after all. That last result breaks the guess, because urban development is human disturbance and the association survived it. So what the wastewater result showed cannot be generalized to human disturbance as a category.

whyWrong.A: No absolute levels of carbon or mercury are compared across the two kinds of disturbed water; the studies concern whether the two vary together.
whyWrong.B: Differing measurement methods would be one way to explain away a conflict, but the text reports no difference in method.
whyWrong.D: How many water bodies each kind of disturbance affects is never discussed and would not explain the pattern of results.

tips: When a third study breaks a proposed rule, the conclusion is usually that the rule was drawn too broadly.

whyCorrect: The sentence lists three readings, and the third is already printed after the blank, joined by "and." So the blank must supply the first two as list items, each ending in a comma — including a comma at the very end, before "and." No comma goes between a temperature and its time, because each reading plus its time is a single item.

whyWrong.A: It leaves off the final comma, so the second item runs straight into "and" and the three-item list loses its separator.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon is used to separate list items only when the items themselves contain commas, which these do not.
whyWrong.C: Commas after each temperature split the reading from its time, and the period breaks the list into fragments.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The sculpture," one object, and the sentence states where it is now. That calls for the singular present verb "stands."

whyWrong.A: "Were standing" is plural and past, but one sculpture stands there today.
whyWrong.B: "Have been standing" is plural; the singular form would be "has been standing."
whyWrong.D: "Are standing" is plural and does not agree with the singular subject.

whyCorrect: "By supplying grain, textiles, and tin to societies that lacked these valuable items" has no subject and no verb of its own — it is an introductory phrase. The main clause is "the Neo-Assyrian Empire grew not only in wealth but also in power and influence." An introductory phrase is joined to its main clause with a comma.

whyWrong.A: A period would leave the introductory phrase standing alone as a fragment.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation the modifier runs into the subject with nothing marking the break.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side, and the first part is not one.

tips: If the first half has no verb of its own, it takes a comma, never a period or semicolon.

whyCorrect: The blank modifies "origins," so it needs the possessive form showing whose origins they are — the two words. "Their" is the possessive; the sentence reads that both words trace their origins to books.

whyWrong.A: "There" indicates a place and cannot show possession.
whyWrong.B: "It's" is a contraction of "it is," which would give "trace it is origins," and the subject is plural anyway.
whyWrong.D: "They're" is a contraction of "they are," producing "trace they are origins."

tips: Expand the contraction and read it aloud; if the sentence breaks, the contraction is wrong.

whyCorrect: "Linguist" appears with no article, so it functions as a title fixed directly to the name, and the phrase continues into "of UC Santa Cruz." A title-plus-name unit like this takes no punctuation between the two.

whyWrong.A: A comma splits the title from the name, and the period ends the sentence in the middle, leaving "of UC Santa Cruz" stranded.
whyWrong.B: The comma still makes the name nonessential, which would require a determiner such as "the" before "linguist."
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete sentence, and "and of keen interest to linguist" is not one.

whyCorrect: Notice the comma already sitting before "amplified" in the passage: it is the closing half of a pair around "by allowing the narrative to be shaped by one of their own." That means the blank has to open the appositive and open that interrupter. "Protest, a decision that," does both — the appositive names Anderson's choice, and the paired commas wrap the interrupting phrase before the verb "amplified."

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, "a decision that" attaches to "protest" as though the narrator participated in a decision, and the interrupter is never opened.
whyWrong.B: A period leaves "A decision that...amplified..." as a fragment, and it fails to open the interrupter with a comma after "that."
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires a complete sentence after it, but "a decision that...amplified the agency" is a noun phrase, not a sentence.

tips: An unmatched comma later in the sentence tells you what the blank has to open.

whyCorrect: The two sentences give different voting ages in different countries: 18 in Ethiopia, 16 in Cuba. The second sets a different case against the first, so the transition marks contrast.

whyWrong.B: "Firstly" opens a sequence, but this is the second item, and no ordered list is being built.
whyWrong.C: "For example" would make Cuba an instance of Ethiopia's rule, when Cuba's age is different.
whyWrong.D: "Therefore" claims Cuba's voting age follows from Ethiopia's, which is not a causal relationship.

whyCorrect: Both halves of the sentence illustrate the same definition: a poem that meditates on a specific painting. Hayden's poem takes Monet's Water Lilies, and Pimentel's takes Klimt's The Kiss. The second example matches the first, so the transition signals similarity.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" marks the second case as an exception to the first, but it follows the same pattern exactly.
whyWrong.C: "Hence" would make Pimentel's poem a consequence of Hayden's, which the text does not claim.
whyWrong.D: "Conversely" introduces an opposite case, and there is no opposition between two ekphrastic poems.

whyCorrect: The paragraph asserts that Modernista architects championed nature, then admits that archways and glasswork obviously cannot grow in a forest, then reasserts the claim with "Still." That "Still" is the giveaway: the sentence before it must be a concession. "Granted" is the word that grants an opposing point before the argument resumes.

whyWrong.B: "Furthermore" adds more support, and this sentence works against the claim rather than reinforcing it.
whyWrong.C: "Thus" presents the sentence as a consequence of championing nature, but a building that cannot grow is not a result of that.
whyWrong.D: "Similarly" claims the two sentences run parallel, when the second pushes back on the first.

tips: When the next sentence begins with "Still" or "Nonetheless," the blank before it is almost always a concession.

whyCorrect: To describe how understanding evolved, the sentence must give both the earlier explanation and the later one and show that the second replaced the first. Only one choice names the 2017 grass-fire conclusion and then the newer cometary-explosion conclusion, joined by "but" to mark the shift.

whyWrong.A: This reports only the newer mineral-signature evidence, so no change over time is shown.
whyWrong.C: This gives only the earlier grass-fire explanation and stops before the revision.
whyWrong.D: This says the two studies differed but names neither explanation, so nothing about the content of the change comes through.

tips: "How understanding evolved" needs both the old view and the new one in the same sentence.

whyCorrect: The goal names one figure: how many participants picked an altered version. That number is 13.1%. The sentence that states 13.1% chose an altered version meets the goal directly; the 86.9% figure is about the opposite group and does not.

whyWrong.A: This gives the percentage who chose the unaltered image, which is the complement of what the goal asks for.
whyWrong.B: This describes the setup of the study and reports no result at all.
whyWrong.C: This describes the task and the character with no figures.

commonMistakes: Grabbing the larger, more prominent statistic when the goal specifies the other group.

whyCorrect: The goal is to specify what Bellini contributes to neutrino research, so the sentence needs his name, neutrinos, and what he does with them. Only one choice ties all three together by naming his research on solar and geoneutrinos and what it advances.

whyWrong.B: This defines neutrinos and mentions physicists generally, never naming Bellini.
whyWrong.C: This gives the discovery date and a definition, with no mention of Bellini.
whyWrong.D: This says Bellini is recognized for particle physics research but never connects him to neutrinos.

whyCorrect: The structure "___ though it seemed...eventually yielded" sets up a reversal: the conjecture looked like one thing but turned out otherwise. Since it was eventually proved, what it seemed was unprovable. "Insuperable" means impossible to overcome, which is exactly the impression the proof overturned.

whyWrong.B: "Unequivocal" means leaving no doubt about its meaning, which does not contrast with being proved.
whyWrong.C: "Irreproachable" means beyond criticism, a judgment of conduct rather than of difficulty.
whyWrong.D: "Ineluctable" means unavoidable, and a conjecture seeming unavoidable would not set up any contrast with someone proving it.

tips: "X though it seemed" always means the sentence is about to contradict X.

whyCorrect: The "not only...but also" frame pairs the blank with "illuminate the Pleistocene epoch," so the blank must be another thing the fossil helps researchers do with knowledge. Its object is "steps in the evolution of hominids," so the verb means to make out or identify. "Discern" carries that sense.

whyWrong.A: "Yield" means to produce or give up, and paleoanthropologists do not produce evolutionary steps.
whyWrong.B: "Exploit" means to make use of for gain, which does not fit steps in an evolutionary sequence.
whyWrong.C: "Prioritize" means to rank in importance, and the sentence is about learning what happened, not ordering research goals.

tips: In a "not only...but also" pair, the blank must do work parallel to the verb in the second half.

whyCorrect: "Before yielding to the efforts of" Adiprasito tells you the conjecture resisted proof from 1970 until 2018. So the blank must describe what it did to mathematicians during that stretch: it baffled them. "Confounded" means exactly that.

whyWrong.A: "Appeased" means calmed or satisfied, but an unsolved conjecture frustrated mathematicians rather than satisfying them.
whyWrong.B: "Disregarded" would mean the conjecture ignored the mathematicians, reversing who acts on whom and clashing with decades of attempts to prove it.
whyWrong.D: "Indoctrinated" means teaching a doctrine uncritically, which a mathematical conjecture cannot do.

tips: "Before yielding" signals a long period of resistance — the blank names that resistance.

whyCorrect: The reason clause is doing the work: much of the evidence of Hatshepsut's reign was deliberately destroyed. Missing evidence means gaps, so what we cannot have is a complete account. "Exhaustive" means covering everything, and the sentence says we are unlikely to ever have one.

whyWrong.B: A superficial account needs little evidence, so destroyed evidence would not make one unlikely.
whyWrong.C: An imaginative account does not depend on surviving evidence at all.
whyWrong.D: Lost evidence makes a questionable account more likely, not less, so the sentence would contradict itself.

commonMistakes: Choosing a negative-sounding word without checking that "unlikely to ever have" already supplies the negative.

whyCorrect: The second sentence supplies the measurement that defines the blank: the effect of recent oil shocks on China's GDP was "only slightly greater than zero." Near zero means barely detectable, so at the national level the effects are small. "Subdued" is the word for an effect that is muted.

whyWrong.B: "Variable" would mean the size of the effect swings from case to case, but the example shows one consistently tiny effect, not a range.
whyWrong.C: "Beneficial" would mean oil shocks help national economies, and an effect near zero is neither help nor harm.
whyWrong.D: "Persistent" describes how long an effect lasts, while the evidence given is about how large it is.

tips: Let the number in the following sentence tell you whether the blank means big, small, or changeable.

whyCorrect: The passage has two moves. First it sets up a puzzle: this ammonite is the largest on record and scientists "have been perplexed by its size" since 1895. Then it reports what Ifrim, Gale, and colleagues did about it — examined 154 fossils and concluded the species evolved from a smaller relative and grew larger because size helped it escape mosasaurs. That is a mystery followed by an attempt to explain it.

whyWrong.A: No prior assumption is stated, so nothing is being overturned; what existed before was confusion, not a belief.
whyWrong.C: The Montana and England fossils are both part of one dataset, and the text never ranks which was more informative.
whyWrong.D: P. seppenradensis was discovered in 1895 and is not presented as newly found; the new material is the explanation, not the species.

whyCorrect: The text names a feature of the series — endings that stop abruptly — then reports two responses to it. Some critics call it a fault; others say the books should be read as one continuous work, which makes the abruptness beside the point. The author takes no side, so the purpose is to lay out the trait and the two readings of it.

whyWrong.A: Entertainment value is never discussed, and the passage does not concede that the structures are flawed.
whyWrong.C: The Forsyte Saga appears as a comparison for multivolume form, not as a standard of fame the series should match.
whyWrong.D: No claim is made that Desolation Island is especially complex or that its structure makes it so.

tips: When a text gives "some critics...but other critics," its purpose is usually to present both, not to pick one.

whyCorrect: The passage splits prey two ways: mussels and clams are "high-quality" and reachable only with a stone anvil, while snails are "abundant, energy-poor, easily extractable." Energy-poor means each item delivers little energy, so an otter living on snails has to work through many more of them to reach the same daily energy total that a tool user gets from fewer, richer items.

whyWrong.A: The text credits tool users with avoiding tooth damage, since the stone does the breaking; it gives no reason to expect snail eaters to fare better on teeth.
whyWrong.B: Fitness benefits are attributed to the tool users, so non-tool users are not the healthier group.
whyWrong.D: The passage says hard-shelled prey usually cannot be accessed by biting alone, so otters are not shown eating mussels and clams without tools at all.

commonMistakes: Reading "abundant" and "easily extractable" as advantages while skipping "energy-poor," which is the term the inference turns on.

whyCorrect: Two figures let you compare. A baleen whale can eat up to 30 percent of its mass per day, and the minke tops out near 10,000 kg, which caps it around 3,000 kg of krill. The bowhead is stated to consume as much as 19,800 kg per day. So the bowhead's daily intake is far larger.

whyWrong.B: The 19,800 kg figure belongs to the bowhead alone; a 10,000 kg minke could not eat nearly twice its own mass in a day.
whyWrong.C: Competition for food between the two species is never mentioned.
whyWrong.D: The text says all baleen whales feed on krill, so it gives no reason to think the minke is less likely to eat it.

tips: When a passage gives a percentage rule and a body mass, it usually wants you to multiply.

whyCorrect: The claim is specifically that sophists are shown as overrating their own wisdom, so you need a sophist speaking about himself. Socrates calling what he propounds "any clever dogma about abstruse matters" is self-praise built into his own instructions to a customer, which is the satire the claim describes.

whyWrong.B: Strepsiades is describing the sophists' odd doctrines and their willingness to argue either side, which mocks their honesty and their teaching, not their opinion of their own wisdom.
whyWrong.C: This is a question Socrates puts to a potential customer about the customer's talent, saying nothing about Socrates's estimate of himself.
whyWrong.D: Strepsiades is urging his son to study; no sophist speaks and no self-regard appears.

commonMistakes: Accepting any quotation that makes sophists look bad rather than the one matching the specific charge.

whyCorrect: Schober's claim is about intent: the watercourts were built to foster conch. The most direct way to weaken it is to show the structures could not have done that job. Evidence that their measured dimensions suit fish but cannot maintain the shallow, seagrass-rich conditions sea snails need attacks the claim at its foundation, because a design unable to support conch was unlikely to have been built for them.

whyWrong.A: Greater sea snail diversity inside the watercourts than in food-processing areas points toward the courts hosting snails, which supports Schober rather than weakening her.
whyWrong.B: A decline in open-water abundance after construction says nothing about what the enclosures were intended to do.
whyWrong.C: Conch not forming the majority of shell fragments still leaves conch present and says nothing about purpose; a court built to foster conch could easily trap more fish.

tips: To weaken a claim about purpose, look for evidence that the thing could not serve that purpose.

whyCorrect: Wade's argument has a local claim inside it: these pieces came from the repertoire of a minstrel working near Heege's home. His current evidence only shows the texts were meant for live performance, which does not pin them to that area. References assuming the audience knows Brackonwet and other small villages near Heege supply exactly the missing link between the texts and a local performer.

whyWrong.B: If simple rhyming also appears in texts that were only read, that undercuts one of Wade's performance clues rather than supporting him.
whyWrong.C: Later manuscripts containing the same pieces speaks to their circulation, not to a local minstrel's repertoire.
whyWrong.D: Minstrels performing mainly for elite audiences sits awkwardly with the popular-appeal material in Heege's collection and gives no support to the local-origin claim.

tips: Ask which part of the argument is least supported by the evidence given, then look for the choice that fills that gap.
